did_you_know.text: Did you know? The priests’ ordination ceremony included several kinds of offerings, each connected with a different purpose: atonement, consecration, and a ritual meal.
Did you know? The ordination took place in front of the entire community, not in secret. The people witnessed the appointment of the priests.
Did you know? The ephod was a special garment of the high priest. Scholars often reconstruct it as a short, apron-like garment fastened with a belt.
Did you know? The names “Urim and Thummim” are commonly understood as “lights” and “perfections,” but the Bible does not explain exactly how they were used.
Did you know? The number seven appears often in the Bible and can suggest completeness. Here, the altar was consecrated through seven sprinklings.
Did you know? The word “messiah” comes from the Hebrew root meaning “to anoint” — to apply oil to someone chosen for a special role.
Did you know? Placing hands on the animal’s head was a ritual act that connected the offerers with the sacrifice, rather than being a casual touch.
Did you know? Blood was placed on the ear, thumb, and big toe of the right side. This can be read symbolically as a commitment to listening, acting, and walking in holiness.
Did you know? A tenufah was a ritual movement of lifting or presenting something before God. The priests held the offering portions in their hands during the ceremony.
Did you know? The Hebrew word milu’im is related to the root meaning “to fill,” so “filling the hands” became an expression for priestly ordination.
Did you know? In this ceremony, anointing oil and sacrificial blood were used together and sprinkled on Aaron, his sons, and their garments as part of their consecration.
Did you know? Aaron and his sons were not ordained in a single day: they had to remain at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting for seven days, like a period of training and preparation for their role.
